doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: A clinic exercise: playing with eyes closed
summary: At a clinic he had a student group start 'Softly in the Morning Sunrise' by improvising with eyes closed, and it improved.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: “Softly in the Morning Sunrise.” I think that’s the one they picked. So they started to play the tune and I listened, now how do you want to start this, what do you want to do. And they started the tune and I listened to it and I says cool, okay, all right. Let’s do it again only this time everybody close your eyes. I want to sit quiet for a minute. I want the bass player, drummer, anybody who feels like starting to play, do not think about that melody, don’t think about what key you’re going to be in, don’t think about anything. I don’t care if you just want to make noises. Just I want somebody to start something at any point in time, but I want us to sit here for about two minutes with our eyes closed. And then I want anybody to join in. And anybody else join in. And anybody else join. And once you’re together as a composite and everybody’s kind of blowing, and if you don’t feel like getting in there, don’t. I says once you’re together and you’ve got the swirl

happening and you’ve got something going on, you know where you’re going, you know the melody of the tune, you know the rough tempo that you want to be at, anybody start it. Anybody start time or start the melody. So to make a long story short, I mean there was a little more explanation in there than that, so I sit back and make everybody sit there with their eyes closed, which was fun too because these young kids, none of them started giggling or anything. Only the one girl was self-conscious. Other than that everybody was pretty into it. So then the bass player started and the piano started but just tinkled like minor seconds. Within a short period of time there was a beautiful conclave of sounds that didn’t have a center but it just was beautiful. And then out of there the horn player started to say it, just loose, without time. And they sort of implied the change, the thing came out. The bass player started to lay down a little bit of time and before you know it they were into the tune and a better, much better tempo than they’d picked the first time. They played through the whole thing, their solos, started to do the same thing with — the drummer was taking it out, I mean things were going on and then when they finished the tune they took it out the same way. And I didn’t tell them to do that. They just took it out — they let it just kind of disintegrate. And it was cool. When they finished they looked up and me and they all started laughing. And they had this — first they had this serious look on their faces. And they all started laughing. I says “you guys got out there, didn’t ya?” They says yeah. That was cool. That’s jazz dude. Because right now you can’t do that tomorrow again. You can’t do it the same way. That’s jazz. Don’t try and do it the same way. Don’t ever, ever try and play it the same way. Try and play different. Today you’ll do it real good, tomorrow you won’t. So what?
